metadata.note: Retail salespersons 3.9M and cashiers 3.1M are the second and sixth largest US occupations (BLS May 2025); with first-line retail supervisors 1.12M this bank covers roughly 8 million workers. Covers till and cash accountability, returns and price disputes, shrink including administrative error and internal theft, age restricted sales, planograms, peak trading, and the supervisor and keyholder track.

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and your retail experience.

key_points: Store type and format: big box, specialty, grocery, fashion, electronics, convenience. The pace and the customer are different in each
Scale in numbers: store volume or footfall, team size, how many registers, whether you worked weekends and peak season
What you actually did: register, floor, fitting rooms, stock and replenishment, returns, opening or closing, keyholder duties
One number you owned or influenced: sales per hour, units per transaction, loyalty signups, shrink, customer satisfaction score
Close on availability, because scheduling flexibility is often the real decision
strong_answer_signals: Names the store format, which tells them whether the experience transfers
Gives a number rather than only duties
Raises availability without being asked
avoid: Listing tasks with no result attached
Being vague about weekend and holiday availability
Saying you are a people person with nothing behind it

questions.text: Tell me about a time you gave excellent customer service.

key_points: Pick a moment where you did more than the transaction: found an item at another store, solved a problem that was not your fault, remembered a returning customer
Situation: what the customer actually needed, including what they had not said out loud
Action: what you did, what you checked, who you involved, and how you followed through
Result: what the customer did next. A purchase, a return visit, a compliment to the manager, a review
strong_answer_signals: The customer outcome is specific rather than they were happy
Shows initiative inside the rules rather than breaking them
Mentions following up or closing the loop
avoid: A story where you simply were polite. Politeness is the baseline, not the answer
Giving away discounts you were not authorised to give
Making the story about how difficult the customer was

questions.text: Tell me about a time you dealt with an angry or upset customer.

key_points: Situation: what happened and why they were upset. Be fair to them, since most anger comes from a real problem
Action: let them finish, acknowledge the impact, then move to what you can do. Lower your voice rather than matching theirs
Say what you were authorised to offer and where you escalated to a supervisor
Result: how it ended, and whether they came back
One line on what you learned about preventing it earlier
strong_answer_signals: Listens first and does not argue about whether they should be upset
Knows the limit of their own authority and uses escalation properly
Keeps other customers in mind while handling one
avoid: Telling the customer they are wrong, even when they are
Walking away or hiding in the back
A story where a manager solved it and you only watched

questions.text: Tell me about a busy shift and how you handled it.

key_points: Set the pressure honestly: a sale weekend, holiday trading, short staffing, a delivery landing at peak
Action: how you triaged. Queue first, then the floor, then the stockroom. Ask for help early rather than late
Say how you kept the basics from slipping: greeting, tidiness, signage, till accuracy
Result with a number if you have one: queue cleared, sales figure, no complaints, till balanced
strong_answer_signals: Prioritises the customer facing queue over back of house work
Asks for help before drowning rather than after
Stays accurate under pressure rather than fast and sloppy
avoid: Claiming you never get stressed
Blaming colleagues or the schedule
Ignoring accuracy to move faster

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked well with your team.

key_points: Pick something with a shared goal: a floor reset, a stock take, a sale launch, covering a colleague short notice
Action: what you personally did, including the unglamorous part nobody wanted
How you communicated during it: handover, radio, checking in when you finished your section
Result for the team and the customer, not just for you
strong_answer_signals: Takes on the part nobody wanted
Communicates rather than working in silence
Credits the team while being clear about their own contribution
avoid: A story where you did everything and the team did nothing
Vague teamwork language with no specific action
Criticising former colleagues

questions.text: Tell me about a mistake you made at work.

key_points: Choose something real and recoverable: a till error, a mispriced item, a missed delivery check, a wrong size ordered for a customer
Own it plainly and say how you noticed, or who told you
Action: reported it immediately, corrected it, told the customer if they were affected
Result and the habit you changed so it does not repeat
One sentence on why hiding it would have been worse
strong_answer_signals: Reports it themselves rather than hoping it goes unnoticed
Names the specific habit that changed
No defensiveness and no over apologising
avoid: Saying you cannot think of one
Choosing a fake weakness that is really a strength
A mistake involving cash that you did not report

questions.text: Tell me about a time you sold something a customer was unsure about.

key_points: Situation: what they came in for and what they were hesitating about
Action: ask questions before recommending. What is it for, who is it for, what have they tried, what is the budget
Match the product honestly, including saying when the cheaper option is right for them
Handle the objection you actually heard: price, fit, timing, or uncertainty
Result: the sale, the basket size, or the return visit. And say if they came back
strong_answer_signals: Asks questions before recommending anything
Willing to recommend the cheaper option when it fits
Names the objection and how it was answered
avoid: Pushing the highest priced item regardless of need
Talking about product features without connecting them to the customer
A story where the customer returned the item afterwards

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to follow a policy a customer did not like.

key_points: Set the policy: returns window, receipt requirement, age restriction, price match limits, promotion terms
Action: explain the rule plainly and without hiding behind it. Say what you can do instead
Offer the alternative that exists: exchange, store credit, manager review, a different promotion
Escalate when the policy allows discretion above your level
Result and how you kept the relationship intact even with a no
strong_answer_signals: Explains rather than recites the policy
Offers what is possible instead of only what is not
Knows when a manager can make an exception
avoid: Breaking policy to avoid a difficult conversation
Blaming the company in front of the customer
Being rigid without offering any alternative

questions.text: Tell me about a time you noticed something wrong on the floor and acted.

key_points: Options that show ownership: a safety hazard, a mispriced shelf, an empty display on a promoted item, a security concern, expired stock
Action: what you did immediately and who you told
Show that you did not walk past it, since that is the whole point of the question
Result: the risk removed, the sale protected, the process changed
strong_answer_signals: Acted without being asked
Knew the correct person to escalate to
Treats the store as theirs rather than as someone else problem
avoid: Waiting for a manager to notice
A story where you reported it and never followed up
Handling a safety or security issue in a way that put you at risk

questions.text: Tell me about feedback you received and what you did with it.

key_points: Pick real feedback: too slow at the till, not greeting customers, missing add on sales, untidy section, phone use on shift
Action: how you took it. Asked what good looked like, watched someone stronger, practised deliberately
Result: the measurable change, and how you know it stuck
Say whether you asked for more feedback afterwards
strong_answer_signals: Takes the feedback without defending
Asks what good looks like rather than guessing
Shows the change stuck rather than lasted a week
avoid: Feedback that was really a compliment
Disagreeing with the feedback in the retelling
No evidence that anything changed

questions.text: Walk me through how you handle a return without a receipt.

key_points: Start with the policy, since this is the most common friction point in retail: what the store allows without proof of purchase
Options that usually exist: lookup by loyalty account or card used, store credit at current selling price, exchange, manager override
Check the item condition and whether it is even a store product. Return fraud is real and this is where it happens
Explain the outcome kindly and offer the best available option rather than a flat refusal
Record it correctly so the return is traceable
strong_answer_signals: Knows lookup options before defaulting to refusal
Mentions return fraud awareness without treating the customer as a suspect
Understands when a manager override is appropriate
avoid: Refusing immediately without checking lookup options
Processing a refund to a different card or as cash when policy forbids it
Accusing the customer of anything

questions.text: How do you handle cash and keep your till accurate?

key_points: Count in and count out, and never share a till login. Accountability depends on one person per drawer
Handle notes one at a time, state the amount received out loud, and leave the note on the ledge until change is given. That habit prevents most disputes
Check large notes for counterfeits per store procedure
Do drops to the safe when the drawer exceeds the limit rather than letting cash build up
If it does not balance, report it immediately with what you remember. Do not adjust anything to make it balance
strong_answer_signals: Says the amount received out loud, which is the professional habit
Reports a discrepancy rather than hiding it
Understands drops and drawer limits as loss prevention, not paperwork
avoid: Putting the note straight in the drawer before giving change
Sharing a till login with a colleague to be helpful
Making the drawer balance by adjusting the count

questions.text: What point of sale systems have you used and what can you do on them?

key_points: Name the systems and be honest about depth. Every chain uses something different and they expect training
Say the transaction types you can handle: sales, returns, exchanges, price overrides, split tender, gift cards, layaway or hold, loyalty lookup
Say what you do when the system is down: manual procedure, card terminal offline mode, or pausing sales, per store policy
Mention accuracy habits: scanning rather than typing codes, checking the screen matches the basket, confirming the total with the customer
strong_answer_signals: Honest about which functions they have actually done
Has a plan for the system being down
Learns systems quickly and says how
avoid: Overstating experience on a system they only watched someone use
No answer for a register failure at peak
Blaming the system for errors

questions.text: How do you help reduce shrink and theft?

key_points: Know the three sources: external theft, internal theft, and administrative error. Most stores lose more to the last two than people expect
Floor habits that actually work: greeting everyone including the person who does not want to be greeted, keeping high value areas covered, tidy displays so gaps are visible
Follow procedure on fitting room counts, security tags, and high theft categories
Never confront or chase a shoplifter. Observe, record what you can, alert the right person. Safety first and it is company policy everywhere
Report internal concerns through the proper channel, since employee theft is the hardest and most important one
strong_answer_signals: Names administrative error as a shrink source, which most candidates miss
Knows not to confront or pursue
Understands greeting as a prevention tool
avoid: Saying you would chase or physically stop a thief
Ignoring internal theft as a category
Treating certain customers as suspects based on appearance

questions.text: How do you handle stock, replenishment and stockroom organisation?

key_points: Priority order: sell through gaps on the floor first, then backstock, then the stockroom tidy. An empty shelf is a lost sale
Receiving properly: check the delivery against the manifest, report damages and shortages the same day, do not sign off blind
First in first out rotation, and date checks where the category needs it
Keep the stockroom findable. Time spent looking for stock is the hidden cost in every store
Cycle counts and accurate system counts, because wrong stock numbers cause both lost sales and over ordering
strong_answer_signals: Puts floor gaps above stockroom tidiness
Checks deliveries rather than signing blind
Connects stock accuracy to lost sales
avoid: Leaving a gap on a promoted line
Signing for a delivery without checking
Treating the stockroom as somewhere to hide from customers

questions.text: How do you approach a customer on the shop floor?

key_points: Acknowledge everyone within a few seconds, even when busy. A nod and I will be right with you keeps people from leaving
Open with something better than can I help you, which invites no. Try what are you shopping for today, or comment on the item they are holding
Read the signal: some customers want space, and the right move is to say where you will be
Ask questions to understand the use case before recommending
Close naturally: offer to start a fitting room, hold it at the till, or check another size
strong_answer_signals: Acknowledges quickly even when serving someone else
Uses an open question rather than can I help
Reads when to give space
avoid: Ignoring customers while facing stock
Following a customer around the store
Launching into a pitch before understanding the need

questions.text: What do you know about upselling and add on sales?

key_points: Frame it as completing the purchase rather than adding to the bill. Batteries, a case, a warranty, care products, the matching item
Recommend from the use case you already asked about, so it sounds like advice rather than a script
Time it at the natural moment: while the customer is deciding, or at the till when it is genuinely relevant
Accept the first no gracefully. Pushing after a no costs the relationship and sometimes the original sale
Know the metrics this affects: units per transaction, average basket, attachment rate
strong_answer_signals: Frames add on as service, not pressure
Accepts no the first time
Names the metric it moves
avoid: Reciting a scripted add on to every customer regardless of fit
Pushing an extended warranty a customer clearly does not want
Ignoring the customer signals to hit a target

questions.text: How do you handle a price discrepancy or a price match request?

key_points: Verify first: the shelf label, the promotion dates, the item code. Most discrepancies are a label left up after a promotion ended
Know the store rule on honouring a displayed price and where your authority ends
For a price match, check the competitor terms the policy requires: same item, in stock, identifiable seller, within the window
Fix the cause as well as the transaction. Correct or remove the wrong label so the next customer is not affected
Be transparent about the outcome rather than vague
strong_answer_signals: Fixes the label as well as the transaction
Knows the limits of their own authority
Checks the competitor terms rather than guessing
avoid: Honouring any price a customer claims without verifying
Leaving the incorrect label in place
Arguing with the customer about what the sign said

questions.text: What do you know about visual merchandising and store standards?

key_points: Follow the planogram or the layout guide, since the placement is usually tested and the data is better than instinct
Basics that always matter: full shelves, facings forward, correct signage, clear pricing, clean and lit displays
Sightlines and traffic flow: the entry zone, the promotional ends, the till queue, and the impulse zone
Keep the promoted lines full and prominent, since that is where the marketing spend went
Reset discipline: do it fully, do it on time, and check it from the customer entry point rather than from behind the display
strong_answer_signals: Knows the planogram exists and why it is followed
Checks displays from the customer viewpoint
Connects merchandising to what is being promoted
avoid: Rearranging displays by personal taste
Leaving a reset half finished at open
Ignoring signage and pricing accuracy

questions.text: How do you handle opening and closing procedures?

key_points: Opening: alarm and key procedure, count the tills, check the floor is customer ready, check overnight deliveries, brief the team on the day priorities
Closing: last customer handled properly rather than rushed out, cash up and safe drop, secure the stock and high value areas, tidy for the morning
Security discipline: never open or close alone if policy forbids it, check the building before setting the alarm, and vary the routine where cash is involved
Handover notes so the next shift starts informed
Say that keyholder responsibility is trust, and that you treat the alarm codes and keys accordingly
strong_answer_signals: Treats the alarm and keys as a trust responsibility
Leaves a handover for the next shift
Does not rush the last customer out
avoid: Sharing alarm codes or keys
Closing alone against policy
Cashing up in view of the window

questions.text: How do you handle age restricted or regulated sales?

key_points: Know what is restricted where you work: alcohol, tobacco and vapes, lottery, solvents, knives, certain medicines, and the age for each
Ask for identification every time it is required, using the store challenge policy such as challenge 25. Consistency protects you and the store
Check the identification properly: valid type, date of birth, photograph, expiry, and signs of tampering
Refuse politely and firmly, and record the refusal where the store logs them
Know that the personal liability is yours as well as the company. Never sell because a queue is building or a customer is angry
strong_answer_signals: Applies the challenge policy consistently rather than by judgement of appearance
Knows how to actually check an identification document
Understands the personal legal liability
avoid: Selling because the queue is long or the customer is intimidating
Accepting a photograph of an identification document
Serving a customer who is buying for someone underage

questions.text: What retail numbers do you understand and how do they connect?

key_points: Sales per hour and conversion rate: footfall in, transactions out. A busy store with low conversion is a service problem
Units per transaction and average transaction value, which is where add on selling shows up
Shrink as a percentage of sales, and the three sources behind it
Sell through and stock turn: how fast inventory moves, and what an overstocked slow line costs
Labour hours against sales, which is why scheduling and peak coverage matter so much
Say which of these you personally influenced and how
strong_answer_signals: Connects a metric to a behaviour on the floor
Knows conversion, not just sales total
Says which numbers they influenced personally
avoid: Naming metrics without understanding what moves them
Thinking sales total is the only measure
No awareness of labour cost against sales

questions.text: There is a queue of six customers and you are alone at the till. What do you do?

key_points: Acknowledge the queue out loud so everyone knows they have been seen. That single sentence keeps most people patient
Call for backup immediately through the correct channel rather than trying to be a hero
Keep a steady accurate pace. Rushing causes till errors that make the queue longer
Keep transactions efficient: hold the conversation for when the queue clears, but do not make anyone feel processed
Afterwards, flag the pattern to a supervisor so cover is scheduled next time
strong_answer_signals: Acknowledges the queue verbally
Calls for help immediately rather than late
Stays accurate rather than panicking
avoid: Working faster by skipping steps like age checks or receipts
Ignoring the queue and hoping someone notices
Getting visibly flustered in front of customers

questions.text: A customer wants to return an item that is clearly used and outside the policy. What do you do?

key_points: Look at the item and check the history: purchase date, receipt, loyalty record, and whether it is a fault claim rather than a change of mind
A faulty product is a different conversation from a change of mind, and consumer law may apply regardless of store policy. Treat them separately
Explain what the policy allows and what you can offer instead
Escalate to a manager where discretion exists, and say why you are escalating
Stay calm if they escalate their tone, and keep the conversation away from the queue if you can
strong_answer_signals: Separates a fault claim from a change of mind
Knows escalation is available and uses it appropriately
Moves the conversation away from the queue
avoid: Refusing without checking whether it is a fault
Approving it to avoid conflict
Arguing in front of other customers

questions.text: You see a colleague giving their friend an unauthorised discount. What do you do?

key_points: Recognise it for what it is. Employee discount abuse is theft and it is one of the largest shrink sources in retail
Do not confront them on the floor in front of customers
Report it through the proper channel: supervisor, manager, or the confidential loss prevention line
Report facts only, what you saw, without speculating about intent
Say plainly that staying silent makes you part of it, and that most stores treat non reporting as a policy breach
strong_answer_signals: Knows the reporting channel exists
Reports facts rather than accusations
Understands that silence is itself a breach
avoid: Saying you would keep it to yourself because it is not your business
Confronting the colleague publicly
Warning the colleague so they can cover it up

questions.text: A customer is being rude to you personally. What do you do?

key_points: Stay professional and do not take it personally. Lower your voice and slow down rather than matching them
Focus on the problem: here is what I can do. Redirecting to the solution defuses most of it
Set a boundary calmly if it becomes abusive or personal, and involve a supervisor
You are entitled to be treated with respect. Every store has a process for abusive customers and you should use it
Afterwards, take a moment if you need it and tell your supervisor what happened
strong_answer_signals: Knows they are allowed to involve a supervisor for abuse
Redirects to what can be done
Does not absorb it silently
avoid: Responding in kind
Accepting abuse because the customer is always right
Walking off without telling anyone

questions.text: Two customers need you at once and one of them was there first. What do you do?

key_points: Acknowledge both. The second customer mainly needs to know they have been seen and how long it will be
Serve in order unless one is a quick answer that takes ten seconds, in which case say so out loud so the first customer understands
Judge urgency: a customer with a child in distress, an accessibility need, or a safety issue changes the order and you should say why
Call for support if the pattern repeats through the shift
Never let the visible queue drift while you give one customer a long consultation
strong_answer_signals: Acknowledges the waiting customer explicitly
Explains out loud when they change the order
Recognises accessibility and urgency exceptions
avoid: Serving whoever is loudest
Ignoring one customer entirely
Long consultations while a queue builds

questions.text: A customer asks for an item you do not have in stock. What do you do?

key_points: Check properly before saying no: the system count, the stockroom, recent deliveries, and whether it is in a different size or colour
Offer the alternatives that exist: another branch, order to store, home delivery, a comparable product, or a notification when it lands
Be honest about timing rather than optimistic. A missed promise costs more than the sale
Capture the demand: tell the supervisor if you are getting repeated requests for something
Follow through on anything you promised to check
strong_answer_signals: Actually checks rather than saying we do not have it
Offers a route to still get the product
Feeds repeated requests back to the buyer or manager
avoid: Saying no from memory without checking
Promising a delivery date you cannot confirm
Forgetting to call the customer back

questions.text: You suspect someone is shoplifting. What do you do?

key_points: Do not confront, chase, block, or touch. This is company policy everywhere and it is about your safety
Increase service presence: approach as a helpful colleague, offer assistance, stay visible. Most opportunistic theft stops there
Alert the right person discreetly: supervisor, security, or the store code word
Observe and remember details you can report: description, time, what was taken, direction of travel
Never accuse anyone, and never act on appearance rather than behaviour
strong_answer_signals: Refuses to confront or pursue
Uses service presence as the prevention tool
Judges on behaviour, never on appearance
avoid: Chasing someone out of the store
Accusing a customer
Profiling based on how someone looks

questions.text: The card system goes down during peak trading. What do you do?

key_points: Tell the queue immediately and clearly. Uncertainty empties a store faster than a problem does
Follow the store procedure: offline mode if supported, cash only, or pausing transactions. Do not improvise a workaround with card details
Report it to the manager and to support at once rather than waiting to see if it fixes itself
Keep customers informed with updates and offer to hold baskets so people can come back
When it returns, work through the queue calmly and check that nothing double processed
strong_answer_signals: Communicates to the whole queue immediately
Follows procedure rather than improvising
Checks for double charges afterwards
avoid: Writing down card numbers to process later, which is a serious data breach
Letting customers wait with no information
Waiting to report the outage

questions.text: A customer wants advice and you do not know the answer. What do you do?

key_points: Say you do not know and that you will find out. Guessing is how customers end up with the wrong product and a return
Find out properly: the product information, a colleague who specialises, the manufacturer site, or the manager
Come back within the time you promised, even if the answer is still pending
Learn it so you are not in the same position tomorrow
Where the stakes are high, such as safety, compatibility or medical adjacent products, never improvise an answer
strong_answer_signals: Admits the gap rather than guessing
Comes back within the promised time
Learns it afterwards
avoid: Making up a plausible answer
Disappearing without returning
Guessing on a safety or compatibility question

questions.text: You are asked to stay late or cover a shift at short notice. What do you do?

key_points: Be honest about what you can do. Say yes when you can and give a clear reason when you cannot
If you can only partly help, offer it: an hour, a different day, a swap with a colleague
Ask about the pattern if it becomes frequent, calmly and in the right setting rather than in the moment
Understand why retail runs this way: absence and footfall spikes are unavoidable and cover keeps the store trading
Be the person who helps when it matters, and be clear about the times you genuinely cannot
strong_answer_signals: Honest rather than over promising
Offers partial help rather than a flat no
Raises a recurring pattern in the right way
avoid: Saying yes and then not turning up
Refusing without explanation
Agreeing to hours that break your own commitments and then resenting it

questions.text: How do you run a shift as a supervisor or keyholder?

key_points: Start with a short brief: today target, the promotions, the priorities, who is on break when, and anything from the last shift
Deploy people to where the trade is rather than where they are comfortable. Reassess when the store fills or empties
Stay on the floor. A supervisor in the back office during peak is a lost hour
Keep the basics visible: queue times, floor standards, gaps on promoted lines, till accuracy
Close with a handover so the next shift is not starting blind
strong_answer_signals: Briefs the team rather than assuming they know
Redeploys people during the shift
Stays on the floor at peak
avoid: Managing from the office
No brief and no handover
Doing everything themselves instead of directing

questions.text: How do you coach an underperforming team member?

key_points: Be specific about the behaviour and the standard: not slow, but average transaction time against the target and what good looks like
Find the cause before prescribing: unclear expectations, missing training, a personal issue, or a motivation problem. They need different responses
Coach in the moment on the floor with a short observable change, not only in a formal review
Set a clear expectation with a review date, and follow up when you said you would
Escalate to a formal process only after real support, and follow the company procedure exactly
strong_answer_signals: Names the specific behaviour and the standard
Diagnoses cause before prescribing
Follows up on the date they set
avoid: Vague feedback like you need to try harder
Going straight to formal warnings
Criticising someone in front of customers or colleagues

questions.text: How do you build a schedule that covers trade and works for people?

key_points: Schedule to the footfall and sales curve by day and hour rather than evenly. Most understaffing is a shape problem, not a hours problem
Protect the peaks: weekend afternoons, evenings, delivery days, and promotion launches
Balance experienced and new staff on every shift so training and cover are possible
Give predictability where you can. Unpredictable schedules are one of the biggest causes of retail turnover
Plan for absence with a realistic cover list rather than assuming a full team
Watch the labour hours against sales, since this is where a store makes or loses its margin
strong_answer_signals: Schedules to the trade curve, not evenly
Values predictability as a retention tool
Mixes experience levels on each shift
avoid: Building the rota around personal preference
Publishing rotas late
Cutting hours at peak to hit a labour target

questions.text: How do you handle a customer complaint that has been escalated to you?

key_points: Take it away from the floor if you can, and let them explain fully before you respond
Back your colleague in front of the customer while still investigating properly. Undermining staff publicly destroys the team
Establish the facts, including the system record, before deciding
Decide with the authority you have, explain the reasoning, and be clear about what happens next
Follow up with the colleague afterwards: what happened, what to do next time, and support if the customer was abusive
strong_answer_signals: Does not undermine the colleague in public
Checks facts before deciding
Debriefs the colleague afterwards
avoid: Overruling staff in front of the customer to end the conflict
Deciding without hearing the colleague
Giving a refund without understanding what happened

questions.text: How do you hit sales targets without damaging service?

key_points: Diagnose the gap first: is it footfall, conversion, basket size, or a stock availability problem. Each has a different fix
Availability is often the cheapest win. You cannot sell what is not on the shelf
Coach the behaviours that move conversion: acknowledgement, open questions, fitting room service, till attachment
Share the numbers with the team hourly or daily so it is a shared game rather than a private pressure
Protect service quality. Pressure selling produces returns, complaints and lost repeat custom
Say what you did that worked, with a number
strong_answer_signals: Diagnoses which lever is broken before pushing the team
Uses availability as the first check
Shares numbers with the team
avoid: Pushing pressure selling to hit a weekly number
Blaming the team for a stock or footfall problem
Chasing sales while standards collapse

questions.text: How do you reduce shrink in a store you manage?

key_points: Measure and segment first: external theft, internal theft, and administrative or process error. Fixing the wrong one wastes the quarter
Process discipline is usually the biggest single win: receiving checks, markdown accuracy, waste recording, transfer paperwork, count accuracy
Internal controls without an atmosphere of suspicion: till accountability, refund and void oversight, discount reporting, clear consequences applied consistently
Floor coverage and service presence in the high risk categories
Involve the team. They usually know exactly where it is going, and they will tell a manager they trust
Give the number: shrink reduced from [X]% to [Y]%
strong_answer_signals: Segments shrink before acting
Names refund and void oversight as an internal control
Builds trust so the team reports
avoid: Treating shrink as only a shoplifting problem
Creating a suspicious atmosphere that drives good staff away
Ignoring administrative error

questions.text: How do you keep a team motivated in a high turnover environment?

key_points: Start with the basics people actually leave over: predictable hours, being treated with respect, a manager who is present, and breaks that actually happen
Recognise specifically and quickly. Retail feedback works best on the day, not in a monthly review
Give people ownership: a section, a display, a category, a new starter to train
Show a path. Even a small one, keyholder or department lead, changes how people see the job
Handle the poor performer, because nothing demotivates a good team faster than someone getting away with it
Give the number if you have it: turnover reduced, or tenure improved
strong_answer_signals: Names predictable hours and breaks as motivation basics
Gives ownership rather than only tasks
Deals with the poor performer
avoid: Relying on incentives and pizza while the basics are broken
Ignoring the person everyone knows is coasting
Treating turnover as inevitable

questions.text: How do you handle a health and safety or security incident in store?

key_points: People first: make the area safe, give first aid or call emergency services, and keep customers away from the hazard
Do not put yourself or staff at risk during a robbery or a violent incident. Comply, observe, and report. Property is replaceable
Secure the scene and preserve any evidence or footage
Report through the proper channels immediately and complete the incident record accurately the same day
Support the staff involved afterwards. A robbery or an assault affects people for weeks and this is where managers are judged
Review the cause and change the process: lighting, cash handling, lone working, spill procedure, display safety
strong_answer_signals: People before property, said explicitly
Records the incident accurately the same day
Supports staff afterwards
avoid: Resisting during a robbery
Delaying or softening an incident report
Sending a shaken colleague straight back on the till

questions.text: Why do you want to work in retail?

key_points: Give a real reason: you like the pace, the people, solving something for someone in a few minutes, the variety of a day
Connect it to something you have actually done, in work or outside it
Say what you want to learn or grow into, since retail employers care about who will stay
Be honest if it is partly the hours or the location. Practical reasons are respected when paired with genuine interest
strong_answer_signals: A concrete reason rather than a generic one
Links it to something they have actually done
Honest about practical motivations
avoid: I need a job as the whole answer
Claiming a lifelong passion for retail
Nothing about customers or the team

questions.text: Why do you want to work for this store specifically?

key_points: Show that you have actually been in the store. Mention the layout, the range, the service you received, the way the team worked
Say something specific about the brand: the products, the customer, the values they publish, the way they train
Connect it to you: why this range or this customer suits what you are good at
Mention practical fit honestly, such as location and availability, alongside the real reason
strong_answer_signals: Evidence of having visited the store
Something specific about the brand rather than generic praise
Connects the brand to their own strengths
avoid: Answers that would fit any retailer
Only mentioning the discount
Getting the product range wrong

questions.text: What does good customer service mean to you?

key_points: Define it concretely: being acknowledged quickly, being listened to, getting an honest answer, and leaving with the problem solved
Say that it includes telling someone the truth, including when the answer is no or when a cheaper product is right for them
Mention consistency. Good service on a quiet Tuesday and on a chaotic Saturday is the actual test
Give a short example from your own experience as a customer or as staff
strong_answer_signals: Includes honesty, not just friendliness
Mentions consistency under pressure
Backs it with a real example
avoid: The customer is always right as the whole philosophy
Only describing being polite
No example at all

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in a couple of years?

key_points: Be honest and grounded. Retail employers know not everyone stays forever, and an unrealistic answer is worse than a modest one
If you want to progress in retail, say the step: keyholder, supervisor, department lead, assistant manager, and what you would need to learn
If you are studying or have other plans, say how this role fits alongside them and what you will commit to
Either way, show you intend to be good at this job while you are in it
strong_answer_signals: Honest rather than telling them what they want to hear
Names a specific next step if progression is the goal
Commits to doing this job well regardless
avoid: Claiming you want to be a store director when it is not true
Saying you have no idea
Making clear you will leave at the first opportunity

questions.text: How do you handle standing all day, weekends and holiday trading?

key_points: Be straightforward. You know the job is physical, involves weekends, and gets hardest exactly when everyone else is off
Say how you manage it: footwear, using breaks properly, pacing, hydration, and sleep before a peak week
Be clear and honest about your genuine availability rather than agreeing to everything and failing later
Show you understand why peak matters: the store makes its year in those weeks
strong_answer_signals: Realistic about the physical demand
Honest availability rather than over promising
Understands why peak trading matters
avoid: Claiming no limits at all
Discovering a scheduling constraint after being hired
Complaining about weekend work in the interview

questions.text: Do you have any questions for us?

key_points: Ask what tells you what the job is actually like:
"What does a typical shift look like, and how many people are usually on?"
"How are hours and rotas set, and how far ahead are they published?"
"What does training look like in the first few weeks?"
"What is the busiest period here, and what changes then?"
"Is there a route from this role to supervisor or department lead?"
How far ahead rotas are published is the question that most affects your life and almost nobody asks it
strong_answer_signals: Asks about rota notice, which shows real understanding of the job
Asks about training and progression
Asks about staffing levels per shift
avoid: Having no questions at all
Asking only about pay and discount
Asking something already covered in the advert
